items.title: Joe Paradi Obituary | Turner & Porter Funeral Directors Ltd. | Mississauga, ON
items.summary: Be the first to offer your condolence on Joe’s Tribute Wall Be the first to offer your condolence on Joe’s Tribute Wall Dr. Joseph Charles Paradi, known to family and friends as Joe, passed away on August 4, 2026, in Mississauga, Ontario, at the age of 85, from dementia. Joe leaves behind his loving wife of 61 years, Monika, his sons Joseph (Beth) and David (Sheila), and grandchildren Andrew (Suzie), Laura (Mattheu), and Sophie. He has always been very proud of his family and was thrilled to find out he was to be a great-grandpa in September. Joe was born on January 18, 1941, in Budapest, Hungary. As a son of Hungarian ice dance champions, he perpetuated the family skating legacy by pursuing speed skating as a child in Hungary. Joe, with his parents and brother, George, escaped the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 and after a short time in England, they immigrated to Canada, ending up in Toronto. Joe earned his Bachelor, Master, and PhD degrees from the University of Toronto, an institution that remained central to his life for many years. During the end of his studies, he became an entrepreneur, founding Dataline, one of the first computer services companies at the time. The growth of Dataline tracked an industry that had a profound impact on most Canadian businesses and his ability to evolve with the changes kept Dataline growing and successful. After selling the company, Joe returned to the University of Toronto as a professor focused on entrepreneurship and data envelopment analysis (DEA). He had a love of teaching so that he could pass along his experiences to the next generation of engineers and entrepreneurs. His teaching, mentoring, and public speaking had an impact on thousands of students and faculty over the years. Joe founded the Centre for Management of Technology and Entrepreneurship (CMTE), which has continued to provide the foundation for University of Toronto engineers to learn critical business skills for their future.

items.title: Mississauga becomes first Ontario city to pause new AI data centres, but proponent likely to appeal
items.summary: Chat GPT app icon is seen on a smartphone screen, Aug. 4, 2025, in Chicago. A Mississauga Council decision Wednesday is being heralded as a victory for sustainability in the face of technology’s relentless consumption of finite resources. The company behind a push to construct a Mississauga-based data centre is already vowing to challenge the decision by locally elected officials. Just a month after residents packed a town hall to voice concerns about Mississauga’s first AI data centre, many returned to City Hall, where more than 20 delegations and over five hours of debate concluded with council voting to pause new data centre developments for one year—becoming the only municipality in Ontario to do so. The decision to pause any approvals for at least twelve months came after residents raised questions about the scale of the operation, the impact on local water resources, the electricity drain on the city’s grid, air and noise pollution, the actual density of hardware in the facility and numerous other matters which illustrated just how little is known about these spaces that distant technology corporations seek to plant around the globe. -based real estate firm Prologis, seeking approval for a Zoning By-law Amendment and Site Plan Approval to facilitate a proposed two-storey data centre, approximately 220,015 square feet, at the northwest corner of Tenth Line West and Argentia Road. Since then, the proposal has moved through the City’s Committee of Adjustment and Planning and Development Committee where staff confirmed the proposal was generally consistent with the Provincial Planning Statement and the Mississauga Official Plan, with no fundamental objection to the provisional proposal.

items.title: House of the Week: French Chateau-inspired estate in prestigious Mississauga neighbourhood
items.summary: Mississauga’s no stranger to luxury homes, but few of them draw from historic French architecture like this beautiful estate in Lorne Park. Designed by an acclaimed architect, this extraordinary mansion offers over 8,000 sq. ft of living space and extravagant finishes. Walk Thru + Tour The landmark French Chateau-inspired estate at 1342 Nocturne Court leaves a striking first impression, enough to distinguish it from the many luxurious properties situated in Lorne Park, one of the most prestigious enclaves in Mississauga. The mansion’s exterior is clad in Indiana limestone with elegant stucco accents, and the interior showcases similarly timeless architecture, exceptional craftsmanship, and refined finishes, designed by acclaimed architect David Small. The home’s 8,200 sq. ft of luxurious living space begins with the grand two-storey foyer. Marvel at the majestic Schonbek Swarovski crystal chandelier, while the radiant heated floors, sweeping circular staircase, and coffered ceilings further set the tone of sophisticated living. Explore the main level with its formal living and dining rooms, as well as a walnut-panelled library, dramatic family room with soaring ceilings, fireplace, and expansive Marvin windows letting in an abundance of sunlight. Soaring ceilings and fireplace in the family room Expansive windows bathe every room in sunlight The well-equipped, chef-inspired kitchen features 5 x 10 ft centre island, custom cabinetry, premium Sub-Zero, Wolf and Bosch appliances, spice kitchen, servery, mudroom, and a designer laundry room.

items.title: 13 student-run businesses featured at Square One Mississauga market
items.summary: An upcoming market will feature 13 student-run businesses in Mississauga. Students have faced challenges finding a summer job in the last few years. Last week, the CNE said it received nearly 50,000 applications ahead of its job fair. Youth unemployment in the Greater Toronto Area peaked at nearly 17 per cent in April. But some entrepreneurial students create their own opportunities. Mississauga’s Summer Company program, which is funded by the Government of Ontario, offers people aged 15 to 29 the opportunity to start their own business, the City of Mississauga said in a press release. High school students commit to 280 or more hours while post-secondary students commit to 420 or more hours between May and Labour Day to their summer company. Through training, guidance from IDEA and hands-on experience, they build skills and turn their ideas into real businesses. One example is Jobbli, an online student job board created by a Grade 10 student in Mississauga. This year, 13 students who are part of the program will showcase their businesses at the IDEA Connect Summer Market at Square One Shopping Centre on Aug. 12.

items.title: Remembering the life of MARGARET WITTS
items.summary: WITTS, MARGARET 'CAROLE' (nee HAWTHORNE, formerly PHILLIPSON) Carole passed away peacefully at Margaret's Place Hospice in Dundas, Ontario on Monday, July 27, 2026, at the age of 85. Carole was predeceased by her parents, Alexander and Lillian Hawthorne; her beloved husband, John Witts; her daughter, Kristen Hill; her brother, John 'Jack' Hawthorne and her brother-in-law, Brian Mooney. Carole will be lovingly remembered by her sister, Sharon Mooney; her cherished nephew and niece, Paul and Micheline Mooney (Bill Green), her honorary grandchildren, Savannah, Addie, Harlow and Colton Green; her grandson, Brennan Hill; her great-grandson, Declen; and her dear friends, Jackie Bell (née Chapman) and Maryke van Gendt. Carole was a dedicated mother to Kristen, and an adoring pet owner, starting with her early love of Irish Setters, and ending with her cherished tabby cat, Toffee. Throughout many years, she was a steady presence for her family and friends, and proudly held the role of honorary Auntie and Grandma for many. Carole was fiercely independent, generous, and lived with integrity. She lived a full life, rich with laughter, friendship, art and good Scotch. She was a sharp mind, with a savvy business sense and entrepreneurial spirit. She was an avid skier for many years, loved a good trip to Manhattan or Vegas, and was a die-hard Toronto Blue Jays fan. Carole lived on her own terms until the end, surrounded by love, tenderness, and admiration. She will be dearly missed, yet will live on in the hearts and memories of many. We would like to extend our deepest and heartfelt thanks to Maryke van Gendt, for her enduring efforts in caring and advocating for Carole in her final days. It will never be forgotten. m.

items.title: Mississauga Becomes First GTA City to Move Toward a One-Year Data Centre Freeze
items.summary: According to Mississauga.com, city council voted unanimously on July 29 to direct staff toward preparing an Interim Control Bylaw that would freeze new applications for large data centres for up to a year. The motion, brought forward by councillors Martin Reid and Sue McFadden, targets facilities built for artificial intelligence, hyperscale computing and cloud services, an industry councillors say has grown faster than the city's existing planning rules can handle. During the freeze, staff would review land-use and environmental policies before recommending permanent regulations for the sector. Mississauga.com notes the move makes the city the first in the Greater Toronto Area to take this step, following months of public concern over the scale and impact of proposed data centre projects. Council is set to consider final approval of the bylaw at its September 16 meeting. Until then, the city's existing rules remain in place, but any new large-scale data centre proposal would face this pending freeze once it takes effect.

items.title: One of Ontario's Oldest Log Homes Marks 200 Years With a Streetsville Celebration
items.summary: The City of Mississauga says the Leslie Log House, built in 1826, is marking its 200th anniversary this year as one of the oldest surviving log homes in Ontario. According to the city, the milestone was celebrated with a special event bringing together members of council, city staff, representatives from the Streetsville Historical Society, and local heritage enthusiasts. The Leslie Log House is a designated heritage property that the city operates in partnership with the Streetsville Historical Society, offering visitors a look at daily life in early Upper Canada. City officials describe the site as an important reminder of Mississauga's rural and agricultural roots, predating the city's later suburban growth by nearly two centuries. Alongside the anniversary celebration, ongoing community programming at the site includes a tea room and art activities in the surrounding park. The city points residents to its website for further details on visiting hours and upcoming programming at the Log House.
